catalog_quote: The accent in Boondéi words falls upon the last syllable but one. Monosyllabic words are, as a rule, suffixed to the preceding word, and the accent is then thrown back, as— Mwengádu, only one, in place of Mwénga dú. The following are the most important:— -si, earth. -hya, new. -du, only. -ngwa, other people's. -ni or -i, the sign of the locative case.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on the held page image of Woodward 1882 p. 2; C&K ROA-176 (held) supports only the tone note. (2) Deciding source is an 1882 missionary grammar sketch; it is old but by the acknowledged authority of the time, and nothing later contradicts it: Meinhof 1906 (fetched sources now from archive.org, MSOS Jg. IX pp. 278-284) is silent on accent and defers to Woodward; modern tonal work (C&K 1997/98 held; Lamont 2025 fetched sources, open access) shows H-tone barred from final position and shifted to the penult plus phrase-penultimate vowel lengthening, i.e. right-edge penultimate prominence consistent with the trochaic-penult coding, though framed at the phrase level as in Swahili-type NE Coastal Bantu. High tones underlyingly on a verb-final vowel surface on the phrase-penultimate vowel phrase-finally. No stress analysis; penult lengthening is phrase-level.
